\worksheethead

\vspace{8pt}

\typehead{Type A: Identify $p$}{A $p$-series $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k^{p}} = 1 + \frac{1}{2^p} + \frac{1}{3^p} + \cdots$ converges if $p > 1$ and diverges if $0 < p \le 1$. The harmonic series $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac1k$ is the case $p = 1$, so it diverges. For each $p$-series, identify $p$ and determine whether the series converges.}

\textbf{1.}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.235\textwidth}p{0.235\textwidth}p{0.235\textwidth}p{0.235\textwidth}@{}}
\pcell{a}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k^{3}}} &
\pcell{b}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}} &
\pcell{c}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-1}} &
\pcell{d}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-2/3}}
\end{tabular}

\vspace{14pt}

\textbf{2.}\par\vspace{4pt}
\begin{tabular}{@{}p{0.235\textwidth}p{0.235\textwidth}p{0.235\textwidth}p{0.235\textwidth}@{}}
\pcell{a}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{-4/3}} &
\pcell{b}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt[4]{k}}} &
\pcell{c}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt[3]{k^{5}}}} &
\pcell{d}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k^{\pi}}}
\end{tabular}

\vspace{14pt}

\typehead{Type B: Rewrite as a $p$-Series First}{Use exponent rules to write each series as $\sum 1/k^p$, then decide.}

\pproblem{3.}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{\sqrt{k}}{k^{3}}}

\divider

\pproblem{4.}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{k^{2}}{k^{3}\,\sqrt[3]{k}}}

\divider

\pproblem{5.}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{k}\,\sqrt[4]{k}}}

\newpage

\typehead{Type C: Constant Multiples and Shifted Series}{Multiplying a series by a nonzero constant, or adding or deleting finitely many terms, does \emph{not} change whether it converges.}

\cproblem{6.}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{7}{k}}

\divider

\cproblem{7.}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k+5} = \frac16 + \frac17 + \frac18 + \cdots}

\divider

\cproblem{8.}{\sum_{k=10}^{\infty} \frac{3}{k^{2}}}

\vspace{10pt}

\typehead{Type D: Sums of Known Series}{If $\sum a_k$ and $\sum b_k$ both converge, so does $\sum (a_k + b_k)$. If one converges and the other diverges, $\sum (a_k + b_k)$ diverges. If both diverge, \emph{no conclusion} --- look more carefully.}

\cproblem{9.}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left( \frac{1}{k^{2}} + \frac{2}{3^{k}} \right)}

\divider

\cproblem{10.}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left( \frac{1}{k} + \frac{1}{k^{2}} \right)}

\divider

\cproblem{11.}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \left( \frac{1}{k} - \frac{1}{k+1} \right) \qquad \text{(If it converges, find its sum.)}}

\newpage

\typehead{Type E: $p$-Series or Geometric Series?}{In a $p$-series $\sum 1/k^{p}$ the variable $k$ is in the \emph{base}; in a geometric series $\sum ar^{k}$ the variable $k$ is in the \emph{exponent}. Identify each series as $p$-series or geometric and determine whether it converges. If a geometric series converges, find its sum.}

\cproblem{12. (a)}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k^{2}}}

\cproblem{\phantom{12.} (b)}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{2^{k}}}

\divider

\cproblem{13. (a)}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{\sqrt{k}}}

\cproblem{\phantom{13.} (b)}{\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{(\sqrt{2})^{k}}}

\vspace{10pt}

\typehead{Type F: Find the Values of $p$}{Find all values of $p$ for which the series converges.}

\oproblem{14.}{$\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k^{2p-1}}$}

\divider

\oproblem{15.}{$\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{1}{k^{p^{2}}}$}

\divider

\oproblem{16.}{$\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} k^{p+3}$}

\newpage

\typehead{Type G: Why the Harmonic Series Diverges}{}

\oproblem{17.}{Let $s_n = 1 + \frac12 + \frac13 + \cdots + \frac1n$ be the partial sums of the harmonic series. Group the terms
$$
s_{16} = 1 + \frac12 + \left(\frac13 + \frac14\right) + \left(\frac15 + \cdots + \frac18\right) + \left(\frac19 + \cdots + \frac1{16}\right)
$$
to show that $s_4 > 2$, $s_8 > \frac52$, and $s_{16} > 3$. Then explain why $s_{2^n} > 1 + \frac{n}{2}$ for $n \ge 2$, and conclude that the harmonic series diverges.}

\divider

\oproblem{18.}{True or false: ``If $\displaystyle\lim_{k\to\infty} a_k = 0$, then $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} a_k$ converges.'' Explain, using the harmonic series.}

\divider

\oproblem{19.}{Use the Divergence Test to show that $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac{k}{k+1}$ diverges. Can the Divergence Test be used to decide whether $\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} \frac1k$ converges? Why or why not?}
